videos.title: Story of a startup that closed after ChatGPT
videos.description:
What happens when you build an innovative AI product, only to see its features absorbed by ChatGPT and Claude? In this interview, Andrew Warner sits down with Nathan Baschez, founder of Lex, to discuss why the AI writing tool is winding down and what founders can learn from its journey.

Lex started as a better writing experience: a place where people could write while using AI as a thought partner, sparring partner, and idea generator. But as general-purpose AI tools added similar capabilities, competing as a standalone writing product became increasingly difficult.

Nathan shares why helping people improve their writing can be a tougher business than helping people build things they couldn't create before. He and Andrew discuss choosing the right market, building for enthusiastic AI users, and the challenges of creating a sustainable AI business in a rapidly changing landscape.

Most importantly, Nathan explains why founders should pursue what genuinely excites them instead of blindly following conventional business advice. His perspective is a reminder that even when a startup doesn't become a lasting independent business, the experience, lessons, relationships, and judgment gained along the way can be invaluable.

videos.title: Hindsight — The AI Memory That Remembers You Across Sessions
videos.description:
Link to the Resource Vault: https://thenextnewthing.ai/Resources
(There is also a clickable link in my bio)

Link to the full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CQhWqUOouYM

Hindsight is an open-source AI memory system that remembers you across sessions. Plenty of memory tools are trending, and it’s hard to tell them apart, but Hindsight stands out because it’s backed by a real company, Vectorize. That matters if you build your agents or routines around a memory system: if it doesn’t keep getting updated as new models come out, you fall behind and have to switch. A company behind it means ongoing updates and better reliability and maintainability. You can fiddle with the open-source version yourself, or use the cloud service if you’d rather have it hosted and share it with your team. For anyone building with AI coding agents, that makes it an easy memory layer to rely on.

The bigger vision is a universal memory layer for AI agents—one that lets you use the best model for each task while keeping your projects, research, and ideas connected across tools.

videos.title: Turn Claude skills into revenue
videos.description:
Resources: https://thenextnewthing.ai/my-resources

Presented by Zapier: https://zapier.com/

Josh Pigford explains how he grew First Index to roughly $570,000 ARR in under a month using AI to automate most of the work.

Andrew Warner talks with Josh Pigford about First Index, a done-for-you SEO and AEO service that helps companies improve how they appear in Google, ChatGPT, Claude, and other discovery tools. Josh explains how he turned a system he had built for his own sites into a $1,000-a-month service, signed up roughly 30 clients, and built an operation largely powered by Claude, Python, GitHub, Notion, Slack, Google Search Console, and inexpensive SEO data. The bigger lesson is how AI can let one person run a service business that would traditionally require a much larger team—while still keeping a human in the loop for judgment, quality control, and the parts clients simply want handled for them.

Links featured:

First Index — https://firstindex.com/

04:03 - Client Isolation: Keep every client in separate GitHub repos and Claude sessions to prevent context bleed.
04:39 - Client Data: Store research, work logs, Search Console data, references, and AI visibility tracking for each customer.
05:33 - What Actually Gets Optimized: Focus primarily on on-site improvements, content, outreach, and correcting inaccurate information.
07:39 - Client Onboarding: Ingest websites, docs, competitors, positioning, tone, and business goals before creating content.

10:57 - Daily AI Workflow: Automatically decide the highest-impact SEO or AEO task for every client multiple times a day.

16:48 - The One-Person Agency Model: Build a potentially multi-million-dollar service company with one human and an AI-powered operating system.
17:06 - The Bigger Opportunity: Use AI to make humans dramatically more productive instead of trying to remove them completely.
18:18 - Knockoff: Apply the same model to brand-protection work and automate the labor-intensive parts of takedown requests.
21:00 - Human-in-the-Loop Businesses: Automate almost everything while keeping a person responsible for the judgment and legally sensitive steps.
21:27 - Sell the Outcome, Not the AI: Customers care about getting the problem solved, not which models or tools are doing the work.
22:12 - Why It Isn’t Pure SaaS: Some services still require judgment and hands-on execution that customers don’t want to manage themselves.
22:48 - Tracking AI Rankings: Use Notion, GitHub, and automated queries to monitor whether clients appear in LLM-generated answers.
23:51 - Keep the Stack Simple: Josh explains why solving the problem matters more than having a perfectly engineered system.

videos.title: Ghidra  — AI Agents Can Now Use the NSA’s Ghidra to Open a Vault
videos.description:
Link to the Resource Vault: https://thenextnewthing.ai/Resources
(There is also a clickable link in my bio)

Link to the full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kqn_mSjSWMs

Ghidra is the NSA’s free, open-source software reverse engineering framework, and AI agents can now drive it. In this demo, the agent installs Java, builds a small app called “the vault,” and tests it with a wrong password, which gets denied. Then it decompiles the app with Ghidra, spots a hex value in the code, prints it out, and uses it to open the vault it built. Ghidra was released to the public in 2019 and is widely used by security analysts, malware researchers, and students as a free alternative to expensive proprietary tools. Watching an agent chain these steps together on its own shows how quickly AI is changing security work.

This demo used an app the agent built itself. Only analyze software you own or have permission to test.

#Ghidra #NSA #AIAgents #ReverseEngineering #CyberSecurity #OpenSource #AITools

🔗 GitHub: https://github.com/nationalsecurityagency/ghidra

videos.title: REA use cases you'll love
videos.description:
Resources: https://thenextnewthing.ai/my-resources
Presented by Zapier: https://zapier.com/
Andrew Warner tests what Reverse Engineer Anything can actually do by reacting to real software-cloning demos.

Andrew Warner looks at REA, or Reverse Engineer Anything, through a series of YouTube demos showing how coding agents can inspect closed-source apps, understand how features work, and rebuild or adapt them. The episode covers cloning QuickTime Player, TickTick, WhisperFlow, a video editor inspired by CapCut, and Loom, plus using REA to find bugs in your own software. Andrew also digs into the bigger question behind all of this: when does reverse engineering become a legitimate way to learn, customize, or improve software, and when does it cross the line into copying?

00:00 - Reverse Engineer Anything: See how REA lets coding agents inspect closed-source software and rebuild features from it.
01:12 - REA Setup: Install the MCP server and skill that teaches your coding agent how to investigate applications.
01:39 - QuickTime Player Clone: Rebuild QuickTime with more granular playback speed controls and extra features.
03:27 - How REA Works: Use tools like Ghidra, Hopper, and IDA Pro through plain-language agent commands.
04:30 - TickTick Clone: Reverse engineer a task manager and rebuild its task lists, calendar, tags, and workflows.
06:54 - Premium Features: See REA recreate functionality that was hidden behind TickTick’s paid plan.
07:39 - Where the Clone Fails: Look at missing features, UI differences, and the extra prompting still needed.
09:54 - WhisperFlow Clone: Rebuild a voice-to-text desktop app with local transcription and multilingual input.
13:39 - Bug Testing: Use REA on your own app to uncover issues that might not be obvious from reading the code.
16:03 - CapCut-Inspired Video Editor: Build a simpler editor with timeline controls, splitting, captions, and export.
19:21 - Inspiration vs Copying: Andrew explores whether using an existing app as a starting point becomes legitimate once you change the product.
19:48 - Loom Clone: Recreate Loom-style recording, movable camera bubbles, and local file storage without copying the exact UI.
21:00 - Final Take: Andrew weighs the practical value of REA against the ethical questions around cloning software.

videos.description:
Link to the Resource Vault: https://thenextnewthing.ai/Resources
(There is also a clickable link in my bio)

Link to the full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Wsru44p-J14

AnyPS5 is an open-source tool that uses AI to read a PS5 game’s files and convert them into a version that runs natively on Windows or Linux. It isn’t an emulator, which is what makes it different, and it’s taking off even though it only works with one game so far. The big catch is that PS5 games are encrypted on the disc, so the tool can’t work on just any new release. The community is already debating whether this is a glimpse of where AI porting is headed or whether it will get taken down quickly, since Sony’s lawyers are almost certainly paying attention.

This video is for information only, so please respect copyright and only use software and games you have the legal right to use.
